In fact one checks directly from the preceding that\n  $$\\angle LHN=\\angle GBA.$$\n\n5.  Conclusion.  \nComparing with (4) we found\n  $$\\angle LGN=\\angle GBA=\\angle LHN\n    \\quad(\\bmod\\pi).$$\nA well‐known criterion for four points $L,N,H,G$ to be concyclic is that the directed angles at $G$ and at $H$ satisfy\n  $$\\angle LGN=\\angle LHN\\pmod\\pi.$$\nHence $L,N,H,G$ lie on a common circle, as claimed.  $\\boxed{}$\n\nRemark.  The key observations are the two parallelisms coming from the parallelogram $DAEH$, which force right angles at $G$ and allow the two angle‐equalities (2), (3) on $\\omega_{1}$, and then the perpendicularities at $G$ defining $L$ and $N$ which tie everything together in the final cyclicity check.\n```\n\n## Reviewer Note\n\nThe solution is an attempt for angle-chase where there is a mistake in almost every line.\n\n=== artifact_02.md ===\n﻿# artifact_02\n\nCompetition: IMOSL  \nProblem ID: IMOSL_2010_1  \nYear: 2010\n\nBenchmark curation item — source: INSAIT-Institute/OPC. The heart of the proof is the reduction mod p and the observation that a function ℕ→ℤ/pℤ whose zero‐locus is always “shifted” exactly when one argument is shifted must be ℤ‐linear.  The rest is a routine application of the Chinese Remainder Theorem.\n```\n\n## Reviewer Note\n\nA reasoning mistake and a computation mistake.\n\n=== artifact_22.md ===\n﻿# artifact_22\n\nCompetition: IMOSL  \nProblem ID: IMOSL_2020_11  \nYear: 2020\n\nBenchmark curation item — source: INSAIT-Institute/OPC.
